black-beans-from-dried-no-added-fat.title: Black beans, dried, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Black beans are the dried seeds of the common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions. They have a dense texture, a mildly nutty flavor, and a dark brown color. Dried beans are typically prepared by soaking and then boiling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black beans are often called "black turtle beans" and are a staple in Latin American cuisine.
They are rich in anthocyanins, pigments that give them their deep color.
Dry beans can be stored for up to a year in a cool, dry place.
In traditional Mexican dishes they appear in frijoles refritos, enchiladas, and soups.
Black beans provide a good amount of plant‑based protein.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: One cup of cooked black beans delivers about 15 g of protein, making them a valuable plant protein source.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Black beans help replenish iron stores, essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Consuming beans leads to a more stable blood‑sugar response.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is important for DNA synthesis and is especially beneficial for pregnant women.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Dry beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and cooking lower its level.

items.title: Potential gas‑forming effect
items.content: Beans may cause bloating in sensitive individuals; introduce them gradually into the diet.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak dried black beans for 6–8 hours, then boil until tender (about 1–1.5 hours). Use them in soups, salads, chili, side dishes, or as a base for vegetarian patties and dips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored they keep quality for up to 12 months. Cooked beans should be refrigerated and eaten within 4‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Brussels sprouts are small, cabbage‑like vegetables from the cruciferous family. Fresh sprouts are commonly steamed, boiled, or sautéed with added fat, which keeps them crisp and enhances their flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The vegetable is named after Brussels, where it was first cultivated in the 16th century.
It is a rich source of vitamins C and K, as well as folate and dietary fiber.
More than 300 varieties exist, differing in size, leaf color, and taste.
Cooking with butter or olive oil improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
When stored properly in the refrigerator, sprouts stay fresh for 2‑3 weeks.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Compounds such as glucoraphanin and quercetin help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy gut function and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Provides beneficial phytochemicals
items.content: Sulforaphane, formed during cooking, may have anti‑cancer properties.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Brussels sprouts can cause increased gas in people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Interaction with blood thinners
items.content: High vitamin K content may affect the efficacy of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may be allergic to cruciferous vegetables.

items.title: Added fat during cooking
items.content: Sautéing with a lot of oil significantly raises the calorie count.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Brussels sprouts can be steamed, boiled, roasted, or sautéed with a little oil. They pair well with garlic, lemon, balsamic vinegar, and nuts. Before cooking, trim the outer leaves and cut off the stem.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sprouts in the refrigerator in a plastic bag or container, keeping them dry. When stored correctly they stay fresh for 2‑3 weeks. Do not wash before storing to avoid excess moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen fruit juice bar is a frozen fruit snack made from 100 % natural fruit juices, without added sugar or artificial preservatives. It has a soft, slightly melt‑in‑your‑mouth texture and a bright fruit flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bars are flash‑frozen right after juice extraction, preserving most of the vitamins and antioxidants.
They may contain super‑fruits such as acai, blueberry, raspberry and others known for their health benefits.
The frozen format allows storage in the freezer for up to 6 months without quality loss.
Each bar weighs about 50 g and provides roughly 80 kcal, making it an ideal snack for athletes.

items.title: Rich in vitamins C and A
items.content: Fruit juices retain high levels of vitamin C, supporting immunity, and provitamin A, beneficial for vision.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Berries used in the bars contain polyphenols and anthocyanins that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: The water content in the frozen form contributes to maintaining the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The bars contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber from the fruit promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: People allergic to specific fruits (e.g., kiwi, strawberry) may experience reactions.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Although no added sugar is present, natural fruit sugars (fructose) should be considered by diabetics.

items.title: Risk of cold sensitivity
items.content: Eating directly from the freezer may cause oral discomfort in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Keep the bar in the freezer and let it thaw for 5‑10 minutes before eating. It can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, blended into smoothies, or used as a cold dessert component.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight package at –18 °C or lower. Once removed from the package, consume within 2‑3 days to avoid crystal formation and texture changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Fresh mushrooms sautéed in vegetable oil have a delicate earthy flavor. Cooking them in oil retains most of their nutrients while adding calories and improving the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mushrooms are the only food source of vitamin D2, which forms when they are exposed to ultraviolet light.
There are over 10,000 edible mushroom species, but culinary use is dominated by button mushrooms, oyster mushrooms, and porcini.
Mushrooms can accumulate trace heavy metals from soil, so it is important to buy them from reputable suppliers.
Sautéing releases aromatic compounds, making the taste richer than raw mushrooms.
Cooked mushrooms are low‑calorie: 100 g of sautéed mushrooms contain about 120 kcal.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms provide niacin, riboflavin, pyridoxine and folate, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports immune health.

items.title: Contains beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans stimulate immune cells and may help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Vitamin D2 and phosphorus in mushrooms contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When cooked with a modest amount of oil, mushrooms remain a diet‑friendly food.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms, ranging from skin rashes to respiratory symptoms.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt is often added during sautéing; excessive sodium intake can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Toxic look‑alikes
items.content: Only properly identified edible mushrooms should be consumed, as many wild varieties are poisonous.

items.title: Food interactions
items.content: Mushrooms contain vitamin K, which can affect the efficacy of anticoagulant medications.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sautéed mushrooms work as a snack, topping for pasta, rice, omelets, salads, and soups. Combine them with herbs, garlic, or a splash of lemon juice to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh mushrooms in the refrigerator in a paper bag for 1–2 days. Cooked mushrooms should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days; for longer storage, freeze them.

content.title: About
content.content: Greek yogurt with no added sugar, enriched with fruit puree (e.g., strawberry, mango, or blueberry). It is made from whole cow's milk, strained to achieve a thick, creamy texture, and contains minimal lactose.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Greek yogurt contains two to three times more protein than regular yogurt.
Straining removes whey, making the product denser and lower in moisture.
Being sugar‑free gives it a lower glycemic index, beneficial for blood‑sugar control.
Fruit puree is often prepared without added sugars or preservatives.
Traditional Greek yogurt is made from whole milk, though low‑fat versions exist.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A 200 ml serving provides about 15–20 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of probiotics
items.content: Live cultures such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: No added sugar helps keep calorie count low and stabilizes blood glucose levels.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Yogurt supplies calcium for bone health and is often fortified with vitamin D.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: When made from whole milk, it retains omega‑3 and omega‑6 fatty acids.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although some lactose is removed during straining, it may still cause discomfort for highly intolerant individuals.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey should avoid this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some brands add a pinch of salt for flavor; check the label if you monitor sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy it straight from the cup, blend into smoothies, use as a base for sauces, dressings, or desserts. The fruit puree makes it a great topping for granola, nuts, and honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the yogurt refrigerated at 2–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5–7 days. Do not freeze, as the texture may become grainy.
